purpose: Itraconazole is used to treat fungal infections in different parts of your body, including your lungs, nails, mouth, throat, and skin. It can treat serious infections like histoplasmosis and aspergillosis, as well as more common ones like nail fungus and thrush. Your doctor may also use it to prevent fungal infections if your immune system is weak.
how_it_works: Itraconazole works by attacking and damaging the outer shell, called the cell membrane, of the fungus. Without a healthy membrane, the fungal cell leaks and dies. Think of it like poking holes in a balloon — the fungus simply cannot survive without its protective covering.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, or diarrhea are the most common issues. You might also notice headaches, dizziness, or skin rash. Some people experience swelling in the legs or feet, and your liver enzymes may go up, so your doctor may do blood tests to monitor you.
warnings: This medication can rarely cause serious liver problems, so tell your doctor right away if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or unusual tiredness. Itraconazole can interact with MANY other medications — some interactions can be dangerous — so always tell every doctor and pharmacist everything you take. It should NOT be used during pregnancy as it can harm the baby. People with heart problems should use it with caution, as it can worsen heart failure.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on the type of infection being treated. For nail fungus, a common approach is 200 mg once daily for 12 weeks, or pulse dosing of 200 mg twice daily for one week per month. For other infections, doses range from 100 mg to 400 mg per day. Always take capsules with a full meal to help your body absorb it properly, and take the oral solution on an empty stomach.
